rw3-instrument.title: (b) Is --diff-filter=A a defensible instrument for 'which manifest came first'?
rw3-instrument.imperative: Apply to the Commander's use of --diff-filter=A the same skepticism I applied to --follow. Check for multiple A entries (add/delete/re-add), check commit-order vs file-write-order, and cross-check against an independent witness (run.generated_at inside the files). rw3-instrument.finding: (b) THE FRAMING IS RIGHT AND THE INSTRUMENT IS DEFENSIBLE -- and the reason is that the wording is calibrated to what the instrument actually measures. The doc says 'the SECOND manifest ADDED to that context directory'. --diff-filter=A measures exactly addition, so the claim and the instrument are the same statement; the Commander did not overreach from 'added' to 'written' or 'produced'. That is the discipline whose absence sank the previous clause, which claimed an ordering ('the run's first') no instrument in the tree supported. I applied the same skepticism I applied to --follow, and the instrument survives it on three grounds. (1) UNAMBIGUOUS HERE: exactly ONE A-entry and ZERO D-entries for each file, so there is no add/delete/re-add sequence for the instrument to report the wrong element of, and neither path has rename ancestry -- which is precisely the failure mode that made --follow lie last round. (2) CORROBORATED BY A CODE-DISJOINT SECOND WITNESS: run.generated_at INSIDE the two files, stamped by the producer at build time and owing nothing to git bookkeeping, gives the same ordering (02:52:37Z before 03:00:53Z). Two instruments with no shared mechanism agree. (3) SUBSTANTIVELY, not just bookkeeping-wise: e5ccd37 at 2026-08-02T02:29:27Z closed g1-implement, which is BEFORE g1-review.json was generated at 02:52:37Z. So when the spine's producer wrote into that directory, g1-implement was already closed and g1-review was the active gate -- and g1-implement.json exists AT ALL only because g1 was later reopened at bcb0975. 'Second added' is a fact about what happened in the run, not an artifact of when someone chose to commit. GENERAL WEAKNESS, named for the record even though it does not bite here: commit-addition time is an UPPER BOUND on file creation, since a file can sit uncommitted on disk indefinitely, and conversely run.generated_at reflects the LAST write of an overwritten file rather than the first. In my BLOCK I raised the possibility that anchoring to a moment no commit identifies would leave the claim true-but-unverifiable, i.e. would move the defect rather than fix it. I measured instead of assuming, and the measurement goes the Commander's way. Manifest counts (every .agent-work JSON carrying contract/step/files/run) at four revisions: 35d2686^ = 49 total, 47 true, 1 false, 1 field-absent -- an EXACT match to the doc's 49/47/1/1; 35d2686 = 56/51/1/4; f6acc1e = 56/51/1/4; HEAD = 56/51/1/4. So the pinned arithmetic is not merely true of some unrecoverable instant -- it is exactly reproducible from the tree, at 35d2686^, the tree the removal was made ON. And because that is a fixed commit, the numbers can never change again: the decay is genuinely stopped, not deferred. The delta is fully explained and I had already derived it: between 35d2686^ and 35d2686 the g4-implement run committed its own seven manifests, four written before the removal (all true, 47+4=51) and three after (field-absent, 1+3=4), 49+7=56. ONE RESIDUAL, followup-grade, not blocking: 'at the point of removal' is prose with two natural readings, and they give DIFFERENT numbers -- 'the tree the removal was made on' (35d2686^) gives 49/47/1/1, while 'the commit that performed the removal' (35d2686) gives 56/51/1/4. A reader who takes the second reading and checks will conclude the doc is wrong, which is the same failure SHAPE as BLOCKER-1 in a much milder form: a checkable-looking claim that fails under a reasonable reading. The fix is one parenthetical, not a rewrite -- name the revision, e.g. 'as of 35d2686^, the tree the removal was made on' -- after which the sentence is settled by a single command. I am recording this as a followup rather than a blocker because the claim as written is TRUE under the reading the author intended, is reproducible, and the numbers themselves are correct; the defect is that the anchor is named in prose rather than in a revision, which costs a reader a guess, not a wrong belief.
